articles.title: AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis
articles.summary: A powerful new AI system could help doctors detect pancreatic cancer years before it becomes visible on conventional scans. The technology, called REDMOD, identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days before diagnosis and was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists. By spotting cancer-related changes at their earliest stages, it could dramatically improve the chances of successful treatment for one of the deadliest forms of cancer.
articles.content:
An artificial intelligence model called REDMOD can identify extremely subtle changes in pancreatic tissue that may signal cancer long before the disease becomes visible to doctors or conventional imaging technology. According to research published online in the journal Gut, the system can detect early signs of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer.

Researchers believe this technology could help transform pancreatic cancer detection by identifying the disease at a much earlier stage (stage 0), when treatment is more likely to succeed. Instead of receiving a diagnosis after the cancer has progressed to an advanced, potentially terminal stage, patients might have an opportunity to begin treatment while the disease is still treatable.

Although REDMOD outperformed experienced radiologists in the study, more research is necessary before it can be introduced into routine medical care. In particular, the scientists emphasize the need to test the system in patients at high risk, including those experiencing unexplained weight loss or recently diagnosed diabetes.

Why Pancreatic Cancer Is So Difficult to Detect Early

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a low survival rate, largely because it is often discovered only after the disease has advanced. Early pancreatic cancer typically produces few noticeable symptoms, and the changes it causes in pancreatic tissue can be too subtle to detect through standard medical imaging. The cancer can also progress rapidly, making timely diagnosis especially important.

To address these challenges, researchers created an artificial intelligence framework known as Radiomics-based Early Detection MODel (REDMOD). The system analyzes extremely fine patterns in the texture of pancreatic tissue, known as radiomics (radiomics), that are not readily visible on conventional computed tomography (CT) scans.

REDMOD also automatically identifies and outlines the pancreas, separating it from nearby organs and tissues. This process eliminates the need for specialists to manually trace the organ's boundaries, reducing the inconsistencies that can arise when different people perform the task.

AI Finds Hidden Cancer Signals Years Before Diagnosis

To evaluate the system, the researchers examined abdominal CT scans from 219 patients treated at multiple hospitals. At the time of their scans, experienced radiologists had found no evidence of pancreatic cancer. However, every patient in this group was subsequently diagnosed with the disease.

The scans had been taken at different intervals before diagnosis. For 87 patients (40%), the images were obtained 3 to 12 months earlier. Another 76 patients (35%) had been scanned 12 to 24 months before diagnosis, while 56 (25%) had undergone imaging more than 24 months earlier (up to around 3 years). In nearly two thirds (64%) of the patients, the cancer developed in the head of the pancreas.

The researchers compared these images with CT scans from 1243 people who remained free of pancreatic cancer for up to three years afterward. The comparison group was matched according to age, sex, and the dates of their scans.

Patients who eventually developed pancreatic cancer had an average age of 69, with ages ranging from 34 to 88. Those in the comparison group were 64 years old on average, with the same age range of 34 to 88.

REDMOD successfully identified subtle imaging signatures associated with pancreatic cancer an average of 475 days before patients received their clinical diagnoses. These early warning signs had previously gone undetected during routine radiological assessments.

"This temporal window holds profound significance, as attaining such early detection would substantially augment the probability of cure and improved survival," highlight the researchers.

"In fact, modelling studies indicate that increasing the proportion of localized [pancreatic ductal carcinomas] from 10% to 50% would more than double survival rates, thereby underscoring that the timing of diagnosis is the single most critical determinant of survival outcomes," they add.

AI Outperforms Experienced Radiologists

The results also showed that REDMOD was substantially better than experienced radiologists at recognizing early cancer signals.

The AI achieved a sensitivity of 73%, compared with 39% for radiologists. Sensitivity measures how effectively a diagnostic method identifies people who actually have the disease, rather than overlooking genuine cases.

The difference was even more pronounced when researchers examined scans taken more than two years before the patients were diagnosed. In these cases, REDMOD achieved a detection rate of 68%, nearly three times the 23% recorded by radiologists.

The researchers also assessed how well the system could recognize scans from people without pancreatic cancer. In an independent group of 539 patients from several hospitals, REDMOD correctly classified just over 81% of scans as cancer free. It performed even better on the publicly available US National Institutes of Health NIH-PCT dataset (80 patients), correctly identifying 87.5% as free of pancreatic cancer.

Additional testing suggested that the early warning signs detected by REDMOD were consistent over time. When the researchers analyzed scans taken from the same patients several months apart, the system produced matching results in 90 to 92% of cases. This consistency strengthened the evidence that the AI was identifying meaningful changes associated with the disease.

Could AI Transform Early Pancreatic Cancer Detection?

Despite the promising findings, the researchers caution that several questions remain unanswered. One limitation is that the study population did not include a sufficiently diverse range of ethnic backgrounds, which could affect how well the technology performs across different populations.

The system must also undergo prospective testing, particularly among people at increased risk of pancreatic cancer, before researchers can determine whether it will be effective in everyday clinical practice.

Even with these limitations, the findings suggest that AI could eventually help doctors identify pancreatic cancer while it is still at a much more treatable stage, potentially improving survival for patients who would otherwise receive a late diagnosis.

The researchers conclude: "This study validates REDMOD as a fully automated AI framework capable of identifying the imaging signatures of stage 0 [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] in normal pancreas, achieving this with substantial lead times and performance superior to expert radiologists."

They add: "While prospective validation is paramount to confirm clinical utility, the REDMOD framework represents a significant advance towards shifting the paradigm for sporadic [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] from a late-stage symptomatic diagnosis to proactive pre-clinical interception, offering tangible hope for improving outcomes in this challenging disease."

The article provides detailed context on the technology, study results, and implications, fulfilling criteria for positive real-world impact, significance, and substance.

articles.title: Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it
articles.summary: The controversial discovery that our brains can generate new neurons surprisingly late in life is now prompting a rethink of adult brain health, pointing the way to better treatments for stroke, dementia and depression
articles.content:
The controversial discovery that our brains can generate new neurons surprisingly late in life is now prompting a rethink of adult brain health, pointing the way to better treatments for stroke, dementia and depression

Joey Guidone

For seven years, molecular biologist Ionut Dumitru and his colleagues played what felt like the world’s most exhausting game of hide-and-seek.

Yet instead of peeking around doors or under beds, they were examining brain tissue in a lab at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden, looking for something that had long evaded neuroscientists: concrete proof that the adult brain can form new neurons via a process called neurogenesis. Scientists have spent decades debating whether this is possible. As soon as one paper turned up positive clues, another would yield nothing at all.

But it seems the search may finally be over. A slew of new findings, including those from Dumitru and his team, have revealed near-certain evidence that adult neurogenesis occurs in the human hippocampus, part of the brain central to learning and memory. The discovery is forcing us to rethink long-held assumptions about our most indispensable organ, from how it functions to how it changes with age.

Advertisement

Even more exciting is the potential neurogenesis holds for brain regeneration. Some of our most devastating medical conditions, including Alzheimer’s, stroke and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), involve neurons dying at massive scale. If the brain is capable of replacing some of those lost neurons, we may be able to harness and enhance that ability, stimulating neurogenesis to help treat neurological conditions that are currently incurable.

“To many of us, we think the question is no longer whether it exists or not,” says neuroscientist Hongjun Song at the University of Pennsylvania. “It’s, how can we take advantage of that?”

Neurons are the brain’s key messengers, transmitting the signals that underpin our most basic functions, from moving and talking to thinking and dreaming. They form when a stem cell – which can morph into other cell types – transforms into a “parent” progenitor cell, which then births an immature neuron that eventually matures.

Scientists long believed this process played out only during development in the womb and, to a lesser degree, during childhood and adolescence. In other words, humans were born with essentially all the neurons they would ever have. The brain would change in many ways over one’s lifetime – forming new connections between neurons and pruning away those that were no longer necessary – but it wasn’t going to get a windfall of new neurons. Or at least, so we thought.

In the early 1960s, Joseph Altman, a biologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, went against the grain by looking for signs of neurogenesis in adult rats. He injected the animals with a radioactive tracer used to track cell division, then identified cells bearing it in the rodents’ brains, revealing what appeared to be freshly generated neurons.

But the finding was widely panned by the neuroscience community. The idea that adult neurogenesis was impossible “had really been embedded within the scientific literature”, says Fred “Rusty” Gage, a neuroscientist at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in California.

Altman was apparently undeterred, replicating his findings in the brains of additional rats and then cats. Other researchers eventually joined in, finding adult neurogenesis in species such as canaries and monkeys, and discovering that it seemed to play a role in learning and memory – helping birds learn new songs, for instance.

But whether human brains also pump out new neurons remained an open question. You can’t ethically crack open a living person’s skull and dig around in their brain tissue.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

Gage and his colleagues found an ingenious workaround to that problem. In the 1990s, some people being treated for cancer received injections of a chemical called BrdU, which flagged dividing cells so that doctors could monitor disease spread. When five such patients had died, Gage and his colleagues were able to autopsy their brains. Lo and behold, they found BrdU in hippocampal cells – a sign of neurogenesis.

The trouble is that BrdU can sometimes flag cells undergoing repair, not necessarily division. And subsequent studies that used different markers yielded results all over the map. Some showed next to no neurogenesis in the adult brain; others, that the adult hippocampus adds 700 new neurons every single day, on a par with that of a much younger brain.

So, Song and his colleagues pioneered a different approach. Instead of looking for immature neurons with just one or two markers, they analysed the full genetic profile of individual brain cells, searching for the genetic characteristics of freshly generated cells. They discovered immature neurons in people who had died across all stages of life, even up to age 92.

But spotting a young neuron still isn’t enough to prove the adult brain is generating new ones. Neurons can linger in an immature state for a long time, perhaps even an entire lifespan. These Peter Pans of the brain aren’t necessarily created in adulthood; they just aren’t growing up.

The real challenge in proving adult neurogenesis occurs was to capture each stage of the process – and one remained elusive. “Nobody had identified the proliferating progenitors,” says Dumitru. “They could identify immature neurons, they could identify maybe stem cells – so the cells that are at the beginning and end of the trajectory – but nobody identified the proliferating ones.”

To identify these cells, which actually birth new neurons, Dumitru and his colleagues genetically analysed roughly 400,000 brain cells from the hippocampi of people who had died between infancy and adulthood. They used a machine learning model – a type of artificial intelligence – to pinpoint genetic patterns that resembled those seen in progenitors from animals and developing infants.

The researchers almost couldn’t believe it when they spotted the first few progenitors. “It was so difficult to convince ourselves,” says team member Marta Paterlini, a molecular biologist also at the Karolinska Institute.

But after years of testing and re-testing, they finally felt confident their search was over. They found only about 350 progenitor cells – and they weren’t present in all the brains sampled. But by finding any at all, “we showed that there is active neurogenesis” in the hippocampus, says Dumitru. “That cannot be contested.”

Except that, well, some scientists still do. Developmental neurobiologist Arturo Alvarez-Buylla at the University of California, San Francisco, isn’t convinced that machine learning models can reliably categorise cell types. He says the only way to know for certain that adult neurogenesis happens would be to track a stem cell as it transforms into a neuron – a nearly impossible task to do in a living human.

But sceptics like Alvarez-Buylla are increasingly finding themselves outside a coalescing consensus. At least 38 clinical trials related to adult neurogenesis are now under way. “It’s there,” says Sandrine Thuret, a neuroscientist at King’s College London. “The new debate is, what is it for?”

One of the first clues to answering that question comes from the fact that adult neurogenesis appears almost exclusive to the hippocampus, the brain’s headquarters of learning and memory. This region is highly plastic, meaning it can easily reorganise itself and form new connections, helping us to take in and remember new information.

In a study from earlier this year, neuroscientist Orly Lazarov at the University of Illinois College of Medicine and her colleagues found that neurogenesis may play a role in this process. They examined post-mortem hippocampus samples from adults who had Alzheimer’s and adults without cognitive impairments, including “superagers” – people in their eighties or older who had outperformed younger adults on a memory test. On average, superagers had roughly twice as many immature neurons in their hippocampus as adults without cognitive impairments. People with Alzheimer’s had almost none at all.

The finding suggests that neurogenesis is closely linked with cognition and may even stave off its decline. Some of the superagers with an abundance of immature neurons also showed signs of Alzheimer’s in their brains, including the condition’s characteristic plaques and tangles. It is possible that enhanced neurogenesis allows the brain to bypass or overcome what would otherwise contribute to cognitive decline, says Lazarov.

Several studies within the past year have also found neurogenesis is impaired in other conditions like Parkinson’s and depression. The latter finding comes from the lab of René Hen, a neuroscientist at Columbia University, New York, who has spent the past 20 years trying to understand the connection between neurogenesis and depression.

His interest began after coming across a study that showed rats dosed with antidepressants had increased rates of neurogenesis. Curious about whether this could explain how antidepressants work, Hen ran a follow-up experiment and found that if he manipulated rodents’ brains to stop producing new neurons, they also stopped responding to antidepressants. Hen was hooked and has been investigating the link ever since.

He and his colleagues have shown that, at least in animals, hippocampal neurogenesis seems crucial for pattern separation – the ability to distinguish between different objects, situations and emotions and remember them appropriately. This process is impaired in depression, as well as other psychiatric conditions in which neurogenesis may go awry, such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. It may explain why people with depression can tend to overgeneralise, for example, interpreting one bad day as evidence that things will always be bad, says Hen.

Like Alzheimer’s disease, these mental health conditions are also associated with smaller hippocampal volumes. While there are probably multiple factors that contribute to this, it is possible that impaired neurogenesis is one of them, says Hen.

Finding a way to stimulate neurogenesis could, therefore, be a promising treatment approach. Several studies have indicated that already available medications, such as antidepressants and the diabetes medication metformin, could stoke neurogenesis.

But there could be more advanced ways of manipulating the process. For instance, if we can pinpoint why superagers have increased neurogenesis, and why it seems to be protective, we could potentially develop therapies that mimic these effects. “We might be able to provide some kind of shield [against cognitive decline],” says Lazarov.

Harnessing neurogenesis could even treat conditions it isn’t directly involved in, such as traumatic brain injury or stroke. A 2025 study showed that transplanting neural progenitor cells into the brains of mice after a stroke led to the production of new neurons and helped the animals regain lost movement.

Still, it will take years to determine whether any neurogenesis interventions work, and even longer to bring them to market if they do. Song and his team are trying to speed up the process by developing miniature models, or organoids, of the human hippocampus. Because these organoids capture what happens in the living human brain more accurately than animal models, they could make it easier to identify therapies that boost neurogenesis, says Song. Other researchers are trying to develop non-invasive brain-imaging techniques to measure neurogenesis in living people, with similar goals.

There may be simpler interventions, too. “Lifestyle is an easy way of modulating, potentially, neurogenesis,” says Thuret.

Exercise may be one way of boosting neurogenesis in adulthood Vivien Killilea/Getty Images for Swisse Wellness

Research has long shown that neurogenesis increases in rats when they are mentally stimulated, such as by having roommates or fun toys in their cages; people may similarly benefit from enriching activities like socialising or learning a new skill.

Exercise also shows promise, at least in rodents. Gage and his colleagues found that when adult rats run on exercise wheels, they produce more immature neurons than sedentary rodents. They also do a better job navigating a maze, signifying enhanced cognitive performance.

Thuret was curious whether the same could be true for humans. So earlier this year, she and her team exposed human hippocampal stem cells to blood serum taken from adults who had completed a three-month exercise programme and those who hadn’t. But instead of stoking neurogenesis, blood from the exercisers actually reduced the number of stem cells ready to become new neurons.

Thuret is still trying to unravel what this means. But given that it is well established that exercise benefits brain health, it may not necessarily be a negative outcome. It is possible that physical activity helps regulate the pace at which stem cells transform into neurons, reserving some for future development, she says.

It is intuitive to think that if impaired neurogenesis is bad, cranking it up to 11 would be good. But too much neurogenesis could backfire, says Thuret. Cancer, a disease of unchecked cell growth, is a prime example of how more isn’t always better when it comes to the human body.

This is just one reason why indiscriminately turning up neurogenesis probably isn’t a viable treatment option. It is more likely that therapies of the future will be targeted, tweaking neurogenesis in different ways and to different levels to treat various conditions, rather than having an across-the-board fix, says Thuret.

Plus, as far as researchers have been able to tell, neurogenesis is mostly confined to the hippocampus. Many cognitive and psychiatric symptoms originate there, but not all of them. For example, a completely different brain region mediates anhedonia – the inability to feel joy, which is a hallmark of depression. “I don’t think that a drug that stimulates neurogenesis is going to cure anhedonia,” says Hen. “The medicine of the future is probably going to be a medicine where we use multiple drugs, each one targeting specific symptoms.”

Unless, of course, neurogenesis isn’t limited to the hippocampus at all.

After finding progenitor cells in the hippocampus, Dumitru, Paterlini and their colleagues didn’t celebrate for long. Instead, they embarked on a new search, turning their attention to the subventricular zone, another part of the brain that some studies suggest is capable of neurogenesis well into adulthood. The work is in early stages, says Dumitru, but already they have spotted signs of progenitor cells in adult samples of this area – a new game of hide-and-seek has begun.

articles.personality_title: Scientists confirm adult brain can grow new neurons, opening doors for new treatments
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For decades, scientists believed that adults could not grow new brain cells, called neurons. Most thought people were born with all the neurons they would ever have, and the brain only changed by making new connections between existing cells.

**What happened** – Researchers at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden used advanced genetic tools and artificial intelligence to find clear evidence that adult human brains can create new neurons, especially in a part called the hippocampus, which helps with learning and memory. This discovery ended years of debate about whether adult brains could grow new neurons.

**Impact** – This finding is important because many brain diseases, like Alzheimer’s, stroke, and depression, involve loss of neurons. If the brain can make new neurons, scientists could develop treatments to help the brain heal or slow down damage. For example, people who stay mentally active or exercise might boost their brain’s ability to grow new cells. Some medicines already known, like certain antidepressants, may also encourage this process.

**What's next step** – Scientists are now working to better understand how neurogenesis (the growth of new neurons) works and how to safely encourage it. They are developing models of the human brain and new scanning tools to study living people. Researchers are also exploring other brain areas that might grow new neurons and testing treatments in clinical trials.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have confirmed that adult human brains can grow new neurons, offering new hope for treating brain diseases and improving mental health.

articles.personality_title_es: Científicos confirman que el cerebro adulto puede generar nuevas neuronas, abriendo camino a nuevos tratamientos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante décadas, los científicos pensaron que los adultos no podían crear nuevas células cerebrales llamadas neuronas. Se creía que las personas nacían con todas las neuronas que tendrían y que el cerebro solo cambiaba formando nuevas conexiones entre las células existentes.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores del Instituto Karolinska en Suecia usaron herramientas genéticas avanzadas e inteligencia artificial para encontrar pruebas claras de que el cerebro humano adulto puede generar nuevas neuronas, especialmente en una parte llamada hipocampo, que ayuda con el aprendizaje y la memoria. Este hallazgo terminó con años de debate sobre si el cerebro adulto puede crear neuronas.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque muchas enfermedades cerebrales, como Alzheimer, derrames cerebrales y depresión, implican la pérdida de neuronas. Si el cerebro puede crear nuevas neuronas, los científicos podrían desarrollar tratamientos para ayudar al cerebro a sanar o frenar el daño. Por ejemplo, mantenerse activo mentalmente o hacer ejercicio podría aumentar la capacidad del cerebro para generar nuevas células. Algunos medicamentos, como ciertos antidepresivos, también pueden estimular este proceso.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos ahora trabajan para entender mejor cómo funciona la neurogénesis (creación de nuevas neuronas) y cómo fomentarla de forma segura. Están desarrollando modelos del cerebro humano y nuevas técnicas de imagen para estudiar a personas vivas. También exploran otras áreas del cerebro que podrían generar nuevas neuronas y están probando tratamientos en ensayos clínicos.

articles.title: Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it
articles.summary: Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body.
articles.content:
Exercise does more than make the heart stronger. New research suggests it also physically reshapes the nerves that control the heart, revealing an unexpected difference between the left and right sides of the body.

Scientists at the University of Bristol (UK) discovered that moderate aerobic exercise changes the structure of nerve cells involved in regulating heart activity. Even more surprisingly, the changes were dramatically different on the two sides of the body. The findings, published in Autonomic Neuroscience, could eventually help doctors develop more precise treatments for irregular heartbeats, chest pain, angina, and stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome.

The discovery was made in rats, so further research is needed to determine whether the same changes occur in humans. Nevertheless, it offers a new perspective on how physical activity influences the nervous system that keeps the heart functioning.

Exercise Changes the Heart's Hidden Control System

The heart is regulated partly by the autonomic nervous system, a network of nerves that automatically manages essential functions such as heartbeat, breathing, and digestion. One branch of this system helps the heart beat faster when the body needs more oxygen, such as during exercise or stressful situations.

Small clusters of nerve cells called stellate ganglia play an important role in this process. Located on both sides of the lower neck and upper chest, these nerve hubs send signals that influence heart rate and other aspects of heart function.

The new research suggests that regular exercise changes these nerve clusters in ways scientists had not previously recognized.

Study lead author Dr. Augusto Coppi, Senior Lecturer in Veterinary Anatomy at the University of Bristol, said: "The discovery points to a previously hidden left-right pattern in the body's 'autopilot' system that helps run the heart.

"These nerve clusters act like the heart's dimmer switch and we've shown that regular, moderate exercise remodels that switch in a side-specific way. This could help explain why some treatments work better on one side than the other and, in future, help doctors target therapies more precisely and effectively."

Just 10 Weeks of Exercise Produced Striking Nerve Changes

To investigate how exercise affects these nerve clusters, the researchers examined rats that underwent 10 weeks of moderate aerobic training. Aerobic exercise is physical activity that increases heart rate and breathing, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling.

The study involved researchers from University College London (UCL) in the UK, the University of São Paulo (USP), and the Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP) in Brazil.

The team used advanced three-dimensional analysis techniques known as stereology to examine the nerve cells. This approach allows scientists to estimate the number, size, and distribution of cells within tissues.

The results revealed an unusual imbalance between the two sides of the body. In the trained rats, the cardiovascular nerve cluster on the right contained roughly four times as many neurons as the cluster on the left, a striking difference from the pattern observed in untrained rats.

The nerve cells also changed in size, but in opposite directions. Neurons on the left nearly doubled in size, while those on the right became slightly smaller.

These findings suggest that exercise does not affect all the nerves controlling the heart equally. Instead, it produces distinct structural changes on each side, potentially providing clues about how the nervous system adapts to regular physical activity.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Treatments?

The findings may have important implications for treating conditions involving abnormal nerve activity around the heart.

Arrhythmias occur when the heart beats too quickly, too slowly, or irregularly. Angina is chest pain or discomfort typically caused by insufficient blood flow to the heart muscle. Another condition, commonly called 'broken-heart' syndrome, involves a sudden weakening of the heart muscle that is often triggered by intense emotional or physical stress.

In some patients, doctors treat these problems by reducing excessive nerve signals reaching the heart. Procedures such as stellate ganglion nerve blocks temporarily interrupt nerve activity, while denervation involves disrupting certain nerve pathways.

Understanding how the left and right nerve clusters differ could eventually help physicians determine which side should be targeted for the greatest benefit.

Dr. Coppi explained: "Irregular heart rhythms, known as arrhythmias, stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome, and certain types of chest pain are often treated by dialing down overactive stellate ganglia -- the paired small nerve hubs in the lower neck/upper chest area that send 'go faster' signals to the heart.

"By mapping how exercise changes these ganglia on each side, the study offers clues that could one day fine-tune procedures like nerve blocks or denervation to the side most likely to help. The findings are early-stage and in rats, so clinical studies would need to follow."

What's Next for Exercise and Heart Research?

Although the structural changes were substantial, scientists still need to establish exactly how they affect heart function.

The research team plans to investigate whether the differences between the left and right nerve clusters influence how the heart behaves during rest and physical activity. They also intend to look for similar patterns in other animal models and eventually in humans.

For human studies, the researchers hope to use noninvasive markers, which could provide information about nerve activity without requiring surgery or tissue removal.

If the same left-right differences are found in people, the discovery could help guide more personalized treatments for arrhythmias, difficult-to-treat angina, and stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome.

Dr. Coppi added: "Understanding these left-right differences could help us personalize treatments for heart rhythm disorders and angina. Our next step is to test how these structural changes map onto function and whether similar patterns appear in larger animals and humans."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery that exercise physically reshapes the nerves controlling the heart, revealing side-specific changes. This finding has broad implications for improving treatments for heart conditions such as arrhythmias, angina, and stress-induced heart syndrome, potentially benefiting many people. The research is detailed, focused, and presents a clear positive impact on health and medical treatment.

articles.personality_title_fr: L’exercice modifie différemment les nerfs du cœur de chaque côté, révèle une nouvelle étude
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université de Bristol ont étudié des rats ayant fait 10 semaines d’exercice aérobie modéré comme courir ou nager. articles.title: How vaccines could be about to revolutionise acne treatments
articles.summary: Acne could be caused by our immune systems overreacting to proteins released by skin bacteria. Columnist Michael Le Page looks into the experimental treatments aiming to block this process and prevent or reduce acne
articles.content:
Acne could be caused by our immune systems overreacting to proteins released by skin bacteria. Columnist Michael Le Page looks into the experimental treatments aiming to block this process and prevent or reduce acne

Can we prevent acne by targeting proteins released by C. acnes bacteria? Science Photo Library / Alamy

It’s a cruel twist. Just as we become more concerned about our appearance, our faces start to erupt in great red spots. Pimples cause anguish for many teenagers and can persist into adulthood too. But now two companies are developing vaccines that they hope will revolutionise the treatment of acne. Is an end to the misery at hand?

The main idea behind this new approach is that acne is caused by the immune system overreacting to proteins released by skin bacteria. Triggering the body to produce antibodies against these proteins should block this process and prevent – or at least reduce – acne. Pharma giant Sanofi is preparing for trials in the US and Canada of an mRNA vaccine targeting at least one bacterial protein, while US start-up Armora Biosciences is focusing on a different protein.

Better treatments for acne are certainly needed. “Acne causes a significant emotional burden,” says Tomasz Zastawny at Armora. “It can lead to the development of depression, social isolation and other psychological outcomes as well.”

Advertisement

It has been known for decades that acne is linked to the presence of a bacterium called Cutibacterium acnes, which thrives deep in hair follicles where there is little oxygen. But C. acnes is the most common skin bacterium, present on just about everybody – including those that don’t have acne – so there’s a lot more to it.

One factor is the surge in hormones during puberty, which increases the production of fatty substances in the skin, affecting bacterial growth. But not everyone gets pimply during adolescence, so there seem to be genetic factors involved as well.

“Acne is very complicated. It’s not an infection,” says Richard Gallo at the University of California, San Diego. “It’s an immune problem.”

In other words, while the presence of C. acne doesn’t usually cause problems, sometimes it may trigger a strong immune response inside a follicle. During this response, some cells in the skin actually turn into fat cells and start releasing alarm signals and antimicrobial substances – a process known as reactive adipogenesis. “This is a normal way to fight an infection, but in this case, it’s an inappropriate response,” says Gallo.

What triggers that response? C. acnes can secrete a toxin known as Christie-Atkins-Munch-Petersen factor, or CAMP. The bacteria may ramp up production of CAMP in certain circumstances.

So, Gallo’s team tried vaccinating mice against CAMP, to make the animals produce antibodies that neutralise the toxin. A number of studies by his team suggest this could help prevent or treat acne.

Sanofi has now developed an mRNA vaccine that targets CAMP, possibly along with some other C. acnes proteins – the company hasn’t revealed exactly what’s in the vaccine and, after much back and forth, declined to talk to me about it.

While there have been reports that the Sanofi trial is already underway, it is labelled as “not yet recruiting” as per the latest update on 18 September. This means it may be some time before we know if it works. That said, while these initial trials are primarily intended to establish safety, it should be clear to volunteers within weeks if it is making a difference to their acne – this isn’t like a normal vaccine trial where researchers have to wait months or years for people to be exposed to pathogens.

“We were very, very optimistic that this could be revolutionary for acne therapy,” says Gallo. “We’ll just have to see if it pans out in the human population.”

Meanwhile, Armora is targeting a different protein, called hyaluronidase, based on work by George Liu at the University of California, San Diego. Hyaluronidase is an enzyme that breaks down hyaluronic acid, a large sugar secreted into the spaces between cells. These terms might be familiar because hyaluronic acid is often used as a filler for cosmetic purposes, while hyaluronidase is injected to break down filler that is no longer wanted or if things go wrong.

Some bacteria such as strep B (Streptococcus agalactiae) produce hyaluronidase for similar purposes, to help them invade tissues. There are two main types of hyaluronidase, it turns out. Some break down hyaluronic acid into simple sugars. Others break it up into large chunks that act as an alarm signal to the immune system.

When it became clear that there were two types, Liu’s team searched genetic databases to see which type is found in which bacteria. They found the “simple sugars” type was the most common. The “large chunks” type was limited to a few free-living bacteria, which makes sense because they don’t need to worry about immune systems.

“The exception was acne,” says Liu. C. acnes jumped out to the researchers because it produces both types of hyaluronidase. More precisely, some strains of C. acne produce the simple-sugars type, while other produce the large-chunks one – none produce both, he says.

That made Liu wonder if this was connected to acne. Sure enough, the team showed in mouse studies that large-chunks strains of C. acnes cause acne-related inflammation, while the simple-sugars one slightly reduces inflammation. The team then went to show that a vaccine that stimulates the production of antibodies targeting only the large-chunks form of hyaluronidase could reduce acne in mice, as could inhibiting the enzyme with a small protein.

What isn’t clear is why some strains of C. acnes have evolved to trigger an immune response. One possibility is that it is a way to kill off some of their competitors, says Liu.

He thinks that in people, a vaccine against the large-chunks form of hyaluronidase would be most effective against the “more severe, red, angry type of acne lesion”.

“The ones that are hard to treat right now, those are the ones that we would target with a vaccine,” he says.

His findings might also help explain why antibiotics, which are commonly prescribed for acne, don’t work that well: they kill off the helpful C. acnes strains as well as the harmful ones. The other issue with antibiotics, of course, is that resistance can develop.

Another acne treatment called isotretinoin (Roaccutane) is more effective than antibiotics but has a long list of nasty side effects including causing birth defects, impotence and dry, itchy skin. How it works isn’t clear, though there is some evidence it alters the skin microbiome.

Acne vaccines promise to solve all these issues. They shouldn’t have any lasting side effects, nor should there be any issue with resistance, because the vaccines are targeting secreted proteins rather than directly targeting bacteria.

The fact that two competing approaches are being developed is great news for those with acne. If one vaccine doesn’t work, perhaps the other will. And it could be that both will work, or that targeting both CAMP and hyaluronidase simultaneously will prove even more effective than either alone. Maybe, just maybe, adolescence is about to get a little easier.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on promising experimental vaccines targeting proteins from skin bacteria to prevent or reduce acne, which causes significant emotional and psychological burden globally. This represents a potential breakthrough in acne treatment with broad public health impact, addressing a common condition with currently limited and problematic therapies. The article provides detailed scientific context and ongoing clinical trial information, indicating substantive progress.
articles.personality_title: New vaccines aim to stop acne by blocking skin bacteria proteins
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Acne is a common skin problem that causes red pimples and can affect teenagers and adults. It happens partly because our immune system reacts too strongly to proteins from bacteria living on our skin.

**What happened** – Two companies, Sanofi and Armora Biosciences, are developing vaccines to stop this immune overreaction. Sanofi is testing a vaccine that targets a protein called CAMP from the bacteria Cutibacterium acnes. Armora is working on a vaccine against a different protein called hyaluronidase. These vaccines help the body create antibodies that block these proteins and reduce acne inflammation.

**Impact** – These vaccines could change how acne is treated by focusing on the immune response instead of killing bacteria with antibiotics. This is important because antibiotics can harm good bacteria and cause resistance. Current treatments like isotretinoin have serious side effects. The new vaccines may offer safer, long-lasting relief from acne, especially the hard-to-treat red and inflamed spots.

**What's next step** – Sanofi is preparing to start clinical trials in the US and Canada to test safety and effectiveness. Armora’s research is still in animal studies but shows promise. If these vaccines work well in humans, they could become a new option for people with acne in the coming years.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Experimental vaccines blocking specific proteins from skin bacteria may soon offer safer, better treatments for acne by calming the immune system’s harmful response.

articles.personality_title_es: Nuevas vacunas buscan detener el acné bloqueando proteínas de bacterias en la piel
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El acné es un problema común de la piel que causa granos rojos y puede afectar a adolescentes y adultos. Ocurre en parte porque nuestro sistema inmunitario reacciona demasiado a las proteínas de bacterias que viven en nuestra piel.

Estas vacunas ayudan al cuerpo a crear anticuerpos que bloquean estas proteínas y reducen la inflamación del acné.

Esto es importante porque los antibióticos pueden dañar bacterias buenas y causar resistencia. Los tratamientos actuales como la isotretinoína tienen efectos secundarios graves. **Resumen en una frase** – Vacunas experimentales que bloquean proteínas específicas de bacterias de la piel podrían pronto ofrecer tratamientos más seguros y mejores para el acné al calmar la respuesta inmunitaria dañina.
